When the flowers reached the bodhisattvas, they were held as appropriate; when they reached the great disciples, they adhered and did not fall. When all the disciples attempted to lift the flowers with their supernormal powers, the flowers would not fall.
The deity asked Śāriputra,
"For what reason did you offer these flowers?
He replied:
"It was not as it should have been; therefore, I raised him. Heaven said, "Not so!"
"This flower is appropriate!
Why does the worthy one say it is inappropriate?
Furthermore, as this flower has neither appropriateness nor inappropriateness, it is merely the worthy one himself who deems it appropriate or inappropriate."
Regarding the observation that the flowers do not cling to the bodies of the great beings: it is because they have abandoned everything, both what is appropriate and what is inappropriate.
For example, when a man is afraid, non-human spirits find an opportunity to exploit him;
because disciples fear birth and death (*saṃsāra*), the objects of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch find an opportunity to exploit them.

For one who has already left behind fear, none of the five worldly pleasures can affect them; though the place of attachment is not yet severed, the flowers merely touch their bodies. For one whose place of attachment is severed, the flowers do not adhere at all.
Śāriputra said, "Heavenly being,
how long has it been since you have dwelt in this room?
She replied:
"Having remained here for so long, you are like those of venerable age who have attained liberation.
He asked again,
"Have you been staying here this long?"
He asked, "Venerable sir, how long has it been since you attained liberation?
Śāriputra remained silent and did not answer.
The deva said,
"Why do you, an elder of great wisdom, remain silent?
He replied:
"One who possesses true understanding has nothing to say or grasp; therefore, I do not know what to say regarding this.
The Deva said:
"If you, Venerable One, speak according to the literal text, then all things would be understood according to their textual characteristics."

Why is this? Liberation is neither internal nor external, nor is it obtained from between the two; likewise, words and letters are also not obtained as something internal, external, or between the two.
Therefore, worthy one!
Do not explain liberation by means of words. Why is this?
"All dharmas are liberated through equanimity.
He asked:
"Is it not further through the absence of desire, anger, and delusion that they are liberated?"
The deva said:

"Those who are extremely arrogant do not achieve liberation through this teaching; rather, it is those who take no pleasure in arrogance—those possessed of lust, anger, and delusion—who attain liberation by means of it.
Śāriputra said:
“Excellent, excellent, O goddess!
By what means and by what realization has your eloquence become such as this?”
He replied:
"I have not attained anything, nor have I realized anything; therefore, my exposition is such as this.
If one were to have attainment or realization, one would be exceedingly arrogant toward the naturally existing Dharma and Vinaya!"
Śāriputra asked the goddess,
"Among the three vehicles, which do you aspire to seek?
The goddess replied:
"Those who practice as disciples ride upon the Dharma of disciples;
those whose conduct follows that of pratyekabuddhas perceive the path with their own eyes;
and those who seek the Great Vehicle personally practice great compassion."
Just as one who enters a sandalwood grove smells only sandalwood and not other fragrances,
so it is, worthy one!
One who dwells in the chamber of the Buddha’s fragrance of virtue does not take pleasure in the fragrance of disciples or pratyekabuddhas.

If devas, nāgas, spirits, Śakra, Brahmā, or the Four Heavenly Kings enter this chamber and hear this noble son expounding the Dharma, they will all delight in the fragrance of the Buddha’s sublime virtues and will never again give rise to the fragrance of sensual pleasures.

In the past, when the Bodhisattva first resolved to leave the household life, I dwelt in this room for twelve years; I heard no miscellaneous talk of disciples or pratyekabuddhas, but only the extraordinary discourse of bodhisattvas concerning the essential principles of the inconceivable Buddha-dharma of great kindness and great compassion.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
this room possesses eight marvelous and spontaneous dharmas that manifest correct transformation.
What are these eight?

This chamber is illuminated day and night by wisdom as one beholds the golden light of the Buddha; it does not take pleasure in the illumination of the sun and moon—this is the first unprecedented marvel.
Those who enter this chamber abide therein with all taints of lust, anger, and delusion forever absent—this is the second unprecedented marvel.
This chamber is constantly filled with Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and bodhisattvas from other lands gathering without ceasing—this is the third unprecedented marvel.

In this room, the discourse on the Path is constantly heard, transforming beings through the wheel of non-retrogression and the six perfections; herein, the Dharma teachings never cease—this is the fourth unprecedented wonder.
In this room, devas and humans perpetually sing sublime music, and from the strings emerge the sounds of immeasurable Dharma transformations—this is the fifth unprecedented wonder.

Within this room there are four great treasuries filled with all manner of jewels, which provide for the destitute and the needy so that their needs are met without end—this is the sixth unprecedented wonder.

In this room dwell Śākyamuni, Akṣobhya, Ratnaśrī, Nandana, Ratnacandra, Ratnaviśuddha, Amita, Dṛḍhadatta, Siṃhaghoṣa, and Prajñākara; when those Tathāgatas and others are remembered by these noble beings or when they are spoken of, those Buddhas immediately come, and upon their arrival, they speak of the conduct of Buddhas such that there is no lack of joy and satisfaction—this is the seventh unprecedented marvel.
This room is pure, and one constantly sees the renowned celestial palaces of the devas as well as the adorned and purified lands of all Buddhas—this is the eighth unprecedented natural phenomenon.
"In this way, worthy one!
This is the correct view of eternalism. Having seen this, who would ever again abandon the training of a disciple?
Śāriputra asked the goddess:
"Why do you not transform out of this female body?
The goddess replied, "It has been twelve full years since I first sought and obtained this female form; indeed, the characteristics of a woman are like an illusion."
"Therefore, one should regard women as illusions and view all things according to their true nature; how then can one speak of 'transforming the female body'?
Śāriputra replied, "One observes that all existing bodies are entirely without substantial reality."
“Thus it is, worthy one!
All dharmas are likewise unestablished; why then do you ask again, ‘How does one transform the female body?
Thereupon, that goddess immediately employed her supernormal power to make Śāriputra stand there appearing like a goddess, while she herself transformed her body into the likeness of Śāriputra.
Having manifested this transformation, she asked:
"Venerable one, how did you come to take on the form of this woman?
Śāriputra, assuming the form of the goddess, replied:
“I do not know by what means I have been transformed into this female form.
The deity said,
“O Worthy One!

If one can transform this female form, then the bodies of all women may likewise be transformed; if, however, one does not perceive even the non-femaleness within a female body, then although all women possess female bodies, they are in fact neither female nor perceived as such.
Furthermore, as the Buddha has said:
"All dharmas are neither female nor male.
At that moment, Śāriputra’s body returned to its original state.
The goddess said:
"Worthy one!
For what reason do you manifest this female form?"
He replied,
"I do not act, yet it is not that I do not act.
The deva said:
"In this way, worthy one!
All phenomena are neither created nor uncreated.
That which is neither created nor uncreated is what the Buddha has taught."
Śāriputra asked the goddess,
"When you pass away from here, where will you be reborn?
The goddess replied:
“I am born as one produced by the Buddha’s transformation; I am born just like that.
He said: “To be born through the Buddha’s transformation is not to be born after having passed away.”
The deva said:
"Sentient beings are likewise; one does not see anyone who dies or is born.
He asked:
“O Celestial One, after how long a time will you be able to achieve the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Path of Supreme Perfect Enlightenment?
He replied:
“It will be as long as it takes for all ordinary people to universally attain the Dharma before I shall achieve Supreme Perfect Enlightenment.”
He asked:
"How is it that when ordinary people universally attain the Dharma, is this not a case of being in the wrong place?
The Deva said:
"That which constitutes unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment has no location. Why is this?
Because the Buddha has nothing established, it is said that there is nothing regarding unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
Śāriputra said:

"Regarding all those Buddhas who have attained supreme perfect enlightenment, those who have already attained it, and those who will attain it—numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges—what are they called?"
He replied:
"This is merely for the sake of those who read according to the numerical sequence of the text; it does not mean that the Way has past, future, or present.
As for the three realms of suffering being equal, take for instance how a worthy person attains the Way."
He replied,
"That which is attained is simply the absence of delusion. Tian said:
"In this way, worthy one!
Even when I have attained Buddhahood, it shall be because they have not yet attained perfect enlightenment.
At that time, Vimalakīrti said to the worthy Śāriputra:

"This deva has already served ninety-two billion buddhas; he has fully realized the wisdom of supernormal powers, his vows are universally fulfilled, he has attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), and he is non-retrogressive. His vows and practices accord with his words, and he is able to manifest whatever he desires."
Chapter 8: The Lineage of the Tathāgata. In the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra, Chapter Eight, "The Lineage of the Tathāgata," Mañjuśrī asked:
"What, noble son, is meant by this?"
“Wherever a bodhisattva goes, there the Buddha-dharma arises.
Vimalakīrti replied, “Wherever they come,
go, and circulate, there wisdom arises and the Buddha-dharma arises.”
"How does a bodhisattva come and go?
When they reach the five places of immediate retribution, they are able to ensure there is no contention or anger;
when they reach the places of hell, they are able to eliminate the darkness and dust."
As for those in the realm of animals, he dispels their darkness and ignorance, enabling them to be free from arrogance;
when they seek entry into the path of hungry ghosts, he provides all manner of merit so that they may be gathered together according to their sequence;
as for those in the realm of the ignorant, he does not return with them, but enables them to know the Way.
In places of anger and malice, he manifests benevolence of mind and does not harm sentient beings;
in places of arrogance, he manifests as a bridge to gather and deliver people;
in places of worldly toil and defilement, he manifests total purity, free from all weariness and impurity.
If one is on the path of the Māras, they can cause those beings to awaken to their objects of perception;
if one is on the path of the disciples (śrāvaka), they enable people to hear dharmas they have not previously heard;
if one is on the path of the Pratyekabuddhas, they are able to practice great compassion and transform others while seated in meditation.
Entering among the poor and destitute, he bestows upon them inexhaustible wealth;
entering among the base and lowly, he causes their lineage to be adorned with marks of majesty;
entering among those of heterodox views, he causes all in the world to take refuge in him.
Pervading all paths, they are able to explain the essential principles for all beings until reaching the path of Nirvana and attaining liberation from birth and death.
Without ceasing, this is the coming and going, the circling, and the entry into all paths by which a Bodhisattva is able to possess the Buddha-dharma.
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti asked Mañjuśrī once more,
“What constitutes the lineage of the Tathāgata?
He replied:

“Existence as a body is the seed; ignorance and craving are the seeds; lust, anger, and delusion are the seeds; the four perversions are the seeds; the five hindrances are the seeds; the six sense bases are the seeds; the seven stations of consciousness are the seeds; the eightfold wrong path is the seed; the nine grounds for resentment are the seeds; and the ten unwholesome actions are the seeds—these are the seeds of the Buddha.”
He asked, "What do you mean by this? Mañjuśrī replied:

"Indeed, one who is empty, non-existent, and beyond number cannot manifest or abide in the arousal of the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment; it is only those dwelling amidst the affairs of worldly affliction who have not yet seen the Truth who can arouse this mind of the Great Way."
For example, son of good family!
On the high ground and dry land, blue lotuses, water lilies, and fragrant *hing* flowers do not grow; it is only in low-lying, damp, and muddy fields that these flowers flourish.

In this way, the Buddha-dharma does not arise from nothingness or non-existence; rather, it is within the midst of afflictions that one perceives sentient beings and gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). Because there is the aspiration for enlightenment, the Buddha-dharma arises. From the point where one perceives one’s own body as being as vast as Mount Sumeru, one is able to perceive others as well and give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment; thus, the Buddha-dharma is born.
Based on this essential principle, one should know that all categories of afflictions constitute the lineage of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, for example, can a person lift up a *niyama-prabhāsa* jewel without descending into the great ocean?
"In this way, how could one who does not enter into the affairs of worldly defilement be able to give rise to the aspiration for omniscience?
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa said:
"Excellent, excellent!"

Mañjuśrī has spoken these words most excellently; it is truly as you intend—that the categories of afflictions constitute the lineage of the Tathāgata. How much more so, then, can the view of a self give rise to the unsurpassed, right, and true path?
Even one who possesses the five deeds of immediate retribution can still give rise to this mind of the Great Way and fulfill the Buddha-dharma;
however, one who has already attained arhatship as an "Arhant" can never again give rise to the mind of the Way to fulfill the Buddha-dharma.

Just as a man whose sense organs are ruined can no longer derive benefit from the five pleasures, so too a disciple who has severed his mixed conduct finds no joy or benefit in the Buddha-dharma and no longer possesses any aspiration for it. Therefore, while ordinary worldlings may still turn back toward the Buddha-dharma, such disciples do not.

Why is this? Because ordinary persons, upon hearing the Buddha-dharma, are able to give rise to the Great Way and ensure that the Three Jewels are not severed; whereas disciples who hear the Buddha’s dharma, powers, and fearlessnesses throughout their entire lives do not again have the intention to give rise to the Great Way.
Thereupon, among those seated in the assembly was a bodhisattva named Drṣṭivicitra, who asked Vimalakīrti:
"Householder!
Where are your father and mother, your wife and children, and your servants, attendants, and staff?"
"Where are your friends, relatives, and servants? To whom do they belong as your followers?

And where are all your elephants, horses, and carriages? At that time, the elder Vimalakīrti answered those who had seen his various forms and spoke in verse: Friends, relatives, and servants— To whom do they belong as my followers?
As for all my elephants, horses, and carriages, Where have they all gone? At that time, the elder Vimalakīrti answered those who had seen his various forms and spoke in verse:
“Mother is the Perfection of Wisdom, father is skillful means;
from these the Bodhisattva is born, attaining the universal vision of a Buddha.
Joy in the Dharma is his wife, and compassion and loving-kindness are his children.”
Receiving the Truths to bring about tranquility, dwelling therein one contemplates the meaning of emptiness.
Learning to know all sensory objects, one’s birth follows as desired;
taking the Supreme Path as a close friend, one awakens the mind without attachment.
My followers are brave and resolute; through the multitude of their attendants, they reach the *apramāṇa* of crossing over.
They fulfill the four debts of gratitude as if serving a woman, delighting in singing the Way and its Virtue.
With *dhāraṇī* as their garden, the flowers of awakening are most marvelous and joyful.
Its fruit is the measure of knowledge and vision; that tree is the great forest of Dharma.
The bathing pool of the eight liberations has its deep pool filled with the water of rectitude;
pure leaves grow there in abundance, where one may bathe free from defilement and dust.
Mounting the chariot of the five supernatural powers, he gallops forth; the Great Vehicle is difficult to surpass.
Guided by the mind of the Way, the Eightfold Path is level and free from sorrow.
His marks are complete to adorn his countenance, and the secondary signs embellish his form.
Through shame and remorse, one avoids unwholesome conduct; the flower garland signifies freedom from doubt.
Of all treasures, this wealth is the greatest: to those who seek it, one bestows both material goods and the Dharma.
Thus one gains vast and manifold rewards and benefits, as one distributes these teachings according to need.
Guarding the teachings through meditative insight, one attains the path of purity free from affliction;
relying thus upon the Buddhas, one’s courageous resolve remains unshaken.
Such a person consumes nectar, taking the flavor of liberation as their drink.
Free from pride and doubt, pure, with the precepts as their unguent;
amidst the dust of those multitudes, they are courageous and invincible;
subduing all Māras, they cause them all to reach the site of enlightenment.
In whatever realm they are born, they are entirely free from the roots of delusion;
they manifest in all buddha-fields to protect and deliver the multitudes of sentient beings.
They make offerings to billions of Tathāgatas and serve the leaders of the three realms.
Not taking me as a model, they become Buddhas; from birth, they are ever intent on fulfilling their cultivation.
They purify Buddha-lands and transform all sentient beings;
through this, they attain the supreme realm where there is no "person" and no "human" conduct.
All classes of sentient beings, their voices and all their various transformations, can be manifested at once;
the Bodhisattva delights in such diligence.
Even those who act with depravity appear in accordance [with his will], being drawn forth according to their desires.
The Perfection of Skillful Means displays all ritual protocols;
it manifests the supreme verbal teachings and demonstrates the end of the body like death.
It blesses and transforms all people and things, never wearying amidst illusory phenomena.
When the kalpa ends and all is consumed by fire, the terrain of the earth is recreated anew;
though people harbor notions of permanence, this illumination makes them realize impermanence.
Even if there were hundreds or thousands of them, they would emerge only as a single village.
They are able to provide empty dwellings for all, establishing them in the gift of the Way.
Just as with the words of a prohibitive incantation, those in various groups within perilous valleys are all brought to the other shore; thus, the Bodhisattva has nothing to fear.
All the various arts and techniques of the world, he studied them all;
not out of following deluded views, but because they served to dispel the confusion of people.
Sometimes he became a sun or moon deity, and sometimes he was the honored one among the Brahmās.
He acts as the lord of the earth through virtue, and likewise as the deity of the wind.
During kalpas of pestilence, he provides medicine;
with diligent compassion, he protects, nurtures, and brings peace, eliminating disease and neutralizing all poisons.
If a famine should occur within a kalpa, one bestows food and drink,
first relieving their hunger and thirst, and subsequently instructs people with the Dharma.
If warfare should break out within a kalpa, one practices compassion and benefit for them.
I transform them through non-contention, so that the myriad people obtain rest and relief.
Even amidst a great war, I gain the multitude of subjects;
they always act in harmony and peace, for the power and majesty of the Bodhisattva are strong.
As for those in prisons and under judicial punishment, there are Buddha-lands beyond counting;
he immediately arrives at each of them to bring peace and security to the multitudes.
Wherever he goes to transform and teach, the five realms of existence are made clearly manifest throughout.
All manner of births appear; this is the birth of a bodhisattva.
Abiding in desire, they manifest abundance; appearing to renounce, they practice dhyāna.
They are able to subdue the leaders of Māra, such that no one knows who holds them fast.
A lotus blooming amidst fire—this may be called rare;
as an incomparable great torch, he acts thus even within the realm of desire.
Wherever people gather in communities, he brings forth the benefits of agriculture for them.
Guided by freedom from greed, established in the wisdom of the Buddha;
seeking to be a leader of the world, a patriarch, or a royal preceptor;
assisting the sovereign and cherishing the subordinates—by these means he brings peace to the masses.
He bestowed bounty upon all the poor, his resources never reaching an end;
according to their needs he practiced giving, exhorting them to give rise to the Way and its Virtue.
Amidst those who were arrogant and conceited, he manifested as a mighty athlete.
He subdues all forms of arrogance and establishes others in the Buddha’s true path.
Seeing those who are in peril or fear, he stands before them to offer comfort;
having bestowed upon them fearlessness, he then transforms them through the reality of the Way.
As a seer possessing the five supernormal powers, he cultivated the practices of Brahma;
he established the multitude in pure precepts, as well as patience, harmony, and the subduing of the mind.
He nourished the people with reverence, so that all who saw him delighted in diligence.
All servants and slaves, he teaches to establish in faith.
Following them according to their capacities and circumstances, he enables people to attain the joy of the Dharma.
Desiring to manifest all that is supreme, he must surely study the profound skillful means.
"This is called practice without limit; therefore, one wanders through the boundless, unites with infinite wisdom, and preaches the Dharma without measure.
Chapter Nine: Entering Non-duality From the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Chapter Nine: Entering Non-duality. Thereupon, Vimalakīrti addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
“Virtuous sirs!
As for what is called ‘the bodhisattva’s dharma-gate of entering non-duality,’ what does this mean?
There was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Dharmakāra who replied:
“Son of good family!

Arising divides things into two; when there is no arising and no birth, then there is no duality. To attain the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) is the entrance into nonduality.”
The Bodhisattva Śūnyatāprativedha said:

"Self and selflessness constitute duality. If there were no such duality, then there would be no distinct appearances; since there is no self, there are no distinct appearances. This is the entrance into non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Animiṣa said:

"To have reception is duality; if one does not receive, there is no attainment. One who has no attainment does not create a deep pool. Being without such activity and without wandering about—this is the entrance into non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Shuli said: "Toiled existence constitutes duality.

For one who rides upon the vehicle of toil, regarding such existence they neither know it nor delight in it; yet, by surpassing all such knowledge while still undergoing form and desire, this is the entrance into non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Sunakṣatra said:

"To conceive of deliberation and non-deliberation as two is duality. One should instead practice by means of neither deliberating nor not knowing; to act while maintaining mindfulness toward all phenomena yet without forming such mental constructions—this is the entrance into non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla said:

“The mind of a bodhisattva and the mind of a disciple constitute duality. If, as I do, one regards all that is experienced with an impartial mind—such that there is no mind of a bodhisattva and no mind of a disciple—and this is identical in character to the absence of mind, this is the entrance into non-duality.”
The Bodhisattva Sunetra said:

"The single characteristic and the absence of characteristics constitute duality. If one does not look at all, does not gaze intently, and does not glance momentarily, neither forming a single characteristic nor a momentary characteristic, but viewing with equal vision whether looking or not looking—this is the entrance into non-duality."
Pongyang Bodhisattva said:

"Good and not-good constitute duality. To be without any arousal regarding good and not-good is called 'non-conceptualization. One who establishes themselves in non-conceptualization does not engage in duality; to be entirely without any crossing over within this state is the entrance into non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Siṃhamati said:
“To not grasp at anything is duality; one should be like a vajra, without cognition or perception, neither acting foolishly nor being a non-understander—this is the entrance into non-duality.”
The Bodhisattva Vigatamati said: "Outflows and non-outflows constitute a duality.

When one attains the True Dharma, the mind becomes equanimous; having attained such equanimity, one ultimately does not form the conceptualization of outflows or non-outflows. Furthermore, this is not attained through the absence of conceptualization, nor does one abide by means of conceptualization or sensation. This is the entrance into non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Viśuddhivimukti said:

"To say 'this has number' and 'this is numberless' constitutes duality. If one departs from all numbers, then the Way and emptiness are equal; when the mind is fully liberated and has no attachments, this is the entrance into non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Janamati said:

"To speak of 'this world' and 'the World-Honored One' as two is dualistic. If the mind regarding this world is empty, and one neither abandons nor dwells upon it, nor relies on the Exalted One, this is the entrance into non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Muki (Direct Vision) said:
"Exhaustion and non-exhaustion constitute duality. That which is exhausted is completely exhausted; that which is completely exhausted cannot be further exhausted—this is called 'inexhaustible.
Because there is nothing to be exhausted, it is called 'exhaustion.'"
He said, "As for 'exhaustion,' there is no exhaustion. One who enters in this manner enters into non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Pubei said, "'Self' and 'non-self' constitute a duality. Since a self cannot be found, how could non-self be found?"
"To be spontaneous with respect to the self and non-acting—this is the entrance into non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Mingtian said:

"Clarity and lack of clarity constitute duality. Because there is an abundance of lack of clarity, there is therefore clarity. If one does not employ or calculate [these], and by means of such non-calculation treats them as equal, attaining the essential point through non-duality within that state—this is the entrance into non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Priyadarśana said: “The world is empty; it is through conceptualization that duality is created.

Form is empty, yet it is not by destroying form that it becomes empty; the very nature of form is emptiness. Likewise, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, yet it is not by destroying consciousness that it becomes empty; the very nature of consciousness is emptiness. One who understands the nature of these five aggregates thus enters into non-duality.”
The Bodhisattva Guangzao said:

"The four elements are one thing and the element of space is another; these two are distinct. Yet the element of space is spontaneous, and the four great elements are likewise so. The original state is spontaneously empty, and the derivative state is spontaneously empty. To know these elements in this way is the entrance into non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Subhāṣita said:
"The eye and forms constitute a duality. One who understands the eye perceives forms without being stained by passion, without anger, and without delusion; this is called purity."

In this way, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena constitute duality. One who understands the mind is unstained by, unprovoked toward, and undeluded regarding these phenomena; this is called purity.
"To abide in this manner is the entrance into non-duality.
Bodhisattva Akṣayamati said:
"To differentiate between giving and omniscience constitutes duality; yet, when giving is spontaneous, omniscience is likewise so."
The naturalness of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is such that giving (*dāna*) is also thus.
Likewise, with respect to ethical discipline, patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom, all-knowledge is divided into two: wisdom is natural, and all-knowledge is also thus;
all-knowledge is natural, and wisdom is also thus.
"To enter into them as one is the entrance into non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Gambhīramati said:

"To regard emptiness as distinct, signlessness as distinct, and wishlessness as distinct is duality. As emptiness is so, signlessness is; as signlessness is so, wishlessness is. That which is wishless is not of the mind, not of the intellect, not of consciousness, and does not engage in activity. To practice with single-mindedness through all gates of liberation—this is the entrance into non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Śāntendriya said: "The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha constitute duality.

The nature of the Buddha is the Dharma; the nature of the Dharma is the Saṅgha. All three jewels are without number; that which is without number is the uncarved block (*prakṛti*). This uncarved block rectifies all dharmas. To delight in following this is the entrance into non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati said:
"To have a body and for that body to be exhausted constitute a duality. To have a body implies its exhaustion. Why is this?
From the body arises views, and from views arises the body."
Therefore, when there is a body, there is destruction and defilement; yet, because it is naturally extinguished without defilement, one who is neither deluded nor confused enters into non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Suprahāna said:
"Body, speech, and mind constitute duality. Why is this so?

This body is of the nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); as the body is unconditioned, so too is the characteristic of speech unconditioned; as speech is unconditioned, so too is the characteristic of mind unconditioned; and as the mind is unconditioned, all phenomena (*dharmas*) are likewise unconditioned."
"That which is without two and without three things is the entrance into non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Puṇyabhūmi said:

"Merit and non-merit, and the act of knowing versus not knowing how to act—these constitute duality. Regarding merit and non-merit, and regarding the state of not knowing how to act, if one is like that [state], there is no such thing as acting; this is non-duality."

Regarding transgressions and blessings, not taking knowledge as having the characteristic of spontaneity (*svabhāva*), but knowing through emptiness—such that it is neither blessing nor non-blessing, yet also not a lack of knowledge—to awaken in this way is the entrance into non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Śubhavyūha said:
"To rely on conditions and engage in verbal expression constitutes duality; if one does not rely on conditions, there is neither that which is unwholesome nor that which is non-wholesome."
"Just as there is neither the unwholesome nor that which is not unwholesome, this is the entrance into non-duality.
Bodhisattva Candraprabha said, "Darkness and light are two;
being neither dark nor light, there is then no duality."

"Why is this? Just as in the meditative absorption of cessation there is neither darkness nor light, so too for one who enters equally according to the true nature of all phenomena—this is the entrance into non-duality.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta.
"To delight in nirvana and not to delight in birth-and-death constitutes duality. If one does not delight in nirvana and does not loathe birth-and-death, then there is no duality. Why is this? "
It is because they are bound by birth and death that they seek liberation; if there were no bondage at all, who would seek liberation?
Thus, where there is neither bondage nor liberation, neither pleasure nor non-pleasure—this is the entrance into non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Mind-Jewel-Establishment said:

"The Great Way and the Small Way constitute duality. One who relies on the Great Way does not delight in the Small Way, nor does he practice amidst the defilements; there is no mark of the Great Way and no mark of the Small Way. For one who is like the practitioner of suchness, there is nothing by which to practice the Way—this is the entrance into non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Chengle仰 (Chénglè Āng) said:
"Sincerity and insincerity constitute duality. One who perceives with sincerity does not see sincerity; how then could they perceive deception and falsehood? Why is this so? [Because]..."
It is not seen by the physical eye; it is seen only through wisdom.
That which is seeing in suchness—neither seeing nor non-seeing—is the entrance into non-duality.
In this manner, after each of the bodhisattvas had spoken, they further asked Mañjuśrī:
"What is meant by the bodhisattva’s dharma-gate of entering non-duality?"
Mañjuśrī said: “As it has been stated, each establishes their own practice;

regarding the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena, there is nothing to grasp, nothing to transcend, nothing to attain, no thought, no cognition, no seeing, and no hearing—this is called ‘entry into non-duality.’”
Chapter Ten: The Buddha of Fragrant Accumulation. In the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*, Chapter Ten, "The Buddha of Fragrant Accumulation," the venerable Śāriputra thought to himself:
"The time for the midday meal is passing; where shall these great beings eat?"
Vimalakīrti, knowing his intention, replied:
"Indeed, worthy one!
If the Tathāgata teaches the practice of the eight liberations, would he do so while being preoccupied with the food of desire?"
"Those who wish to hear the Dharma should first take this as their meal.

At that moment, Vimalakīrti entered the samādhi known as "Just as It Is. In the direction of the zenith, beyond as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in forty-two Ganges Rivers, there was a Buddha named Gandhottamakūṭa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; his world was called Sarvagandhasugandhā.

All the disciples and bodhisattvas saw his land; its fragrance universally perfumed the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, including all devas and humans, and compared to all other Buddha-fields, its scent was the most excellent.
In that world, there are no names for disciples or pratyekabuddhas; that Tathāgata does not preach the Dharma for the sake of bodhisattvas.

Everything in that realm consists of fragrant pavilions, fragrant grounds for walking meditation, and fragrant gardens and groves. The food and drink of the bodhisattvas consist entirely of various fragrances, and these scents circulate throughout immeasurable worlds.
At that time, as the various bodhisattvas of that Buddha were sitting down to eat, there was a son of heaven named Gandhavyuha who had studied the Mahāyāna and remained there in attendance.
The entire great assembly saw the Tathāgata Gandhottamakūṭa and his bodhisattvas sitting and eating. Vimalakīrti then addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"O sons of noble family!..."
"Who is able to bring that Buddha’s meal?
They all replied, "We cannot.
He then asked Mañjuśrī:
“O Minister!
Has this assembly not yet fully understood?
He replied:
“As the Buddha has said, we do not yet know; we shall learn.
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti, without rising from his seat, manifested before the assembly a bodhisattva with a clearly defined radiance and form, and addressed him, saying:
“Go forth from this buddha-field, crossing as many worlds as there are sands in forty-two Ganges Rivers, until you reach the realm of Saugandhika and the presence of the Buddha Gandhottamakūṭa.”
When you arrive and have finished eating, pay homage at the Buddha’s feet and speak on my behalf, saying: "Vimalakīrti says:

'I pray that you will grant me the remains of the World-Honored One's meal. I wish to perform the work of a Buddha within this Sahā world, so that those who are indolent and discouraged may expand their great resolve, and so that the fame of the Tathāgata may be heard everywhere.'"
The manifested bodhisattva then took his place before the assembly, ascended toward the zenith, and suddenly vanished from sight; the entire multitude witnessed his departure.
Upon reaching the World of Fragrant Multitudes, the manifested bodhisattva prostrated at the feet of that Buddha and said:

"The Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti bows his head to the feet of the World-Honored One and respectfully inquires after your immeasurable well-being, your ease of movement, your robust health, and your receipt of blessings and prosperity. He prays that you will grant him the remains of your meal, so that he may perform buddha-work in the Sahā world, enabling those people there who are weary and indolent to expand their great resolve, and causing the fame of the Tathāgata to be heard everywhere."
Those bodhisattvas were all struck with astonishment and said:
"Where has this person come from?
In what world could there be such a person who is indolent and negligent?"
He immediately asked the Buddha about this.
Fragrant Accumulation replied:

"Below this world, passing through as many buddha-fields as there are sands in forty-two Ganges Rivers, lies the Sahā world. There is a Buddha named Śākyamuni—translated into Chinese as Nengren (Capable Benevolence)—a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
"In this world-system of five turbidities, he uses the Dharma to instruct those who are indolent and negligent.
There is a bodhisattva there named Vimalakīrti who speaks of the sublime Dharma; he has now sent a transformation-body here to extol my name."
That bodhisattva asked:
"What kind of person is it that can perform such transformations, possessing such power of virtue and fearlessness, and such supernormal faculties?
The Buddha said:
"Extremely great!
He dispatches emanations to all worlds, performing the works of a Buddha to establish the multitude.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata Gandhottama-kūṭa took a bowl filled with fragrant food and all manner of fragrant implements and gave them to the emanated bodhisattvas.
Then, those ninety thousand bodhisattvas spoke with one voice, saying:
"We wish to go to the Land of Endurance to see Śākyamuni.
That Buddha replied:
"Go, son of good family!

Take this incense of forbearance and enter that world. Do not, out of a sense of benevolence toward them, harbor thoughts of negligence; maintain your own preferred practice and do not think that the bodhisattvas of that land are inferior. Do not give rise to thoughts of despondency or weariness regarding them."
"Why is this? The Buddha-fields are empty;
it is only because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, desire to deliver sentient beings that they manifest those lands.

Having accepted the food, the transformed bodhisattvas, together with the great beings, received the holy intent of the Buddha and the transformation of Vimalakīrti, and in an instant returned from there to Vimalakīrti’s house.

Vimalakīrti then miraculously transformed himself into ninety thousand lion thrones, as magnificent and beautiful as before. Once all the bodhisattvas were seated, the manifested bodhisattva presented the Buddha’s complete meal to Vimalakīrti. The fragrance of the food permeated the entire city of Vaiśālī, and a sublime scent filled the entire trichiliocosm.

At that time, the brahmins, householders, and the venerable ones of Vaiśālī, such as Candracchattra and others, upon smelling this fragrance, all attained a state of unprecedented, spontaneous realization; their bodies and minds were filled with joy and serenity.

Eighty-four thousand people entered the house of Vimalakīrti. Observing that there were many bodhisattvas within the room and beholding the lion thrones—lofty, magnificent, and beautiful—they all rejoiced greatly. They paid homage to the bodhisattvas and the great disciples, then withdrew to stand to one side.
The devas of the Fragrant Grounds and the devas of the Realm of Form all came to the house.
Vimalakīrti addressed the elder Śāriputra and the other great disciples, saying:
"Venerable ones!..."
"You may eat the Tathāgata’s rice; it possesses only the flavor of great compassion, and there is no limited practice that binds the mind.
A certain disciple thought to himself, "This rice is little, yet this great assembly must each eat their fill."
The transformed bodhisattva said:
"The four oceans may run dry, but this food is inexhaustible; even if all people were to eat morsels as large as Mount Sumeru, it still could not be exhausted—it is truly imperishable."
Why is this? Because there is no exhaustion of the precepts, nor of concentration and wisdom, nor of liberation, knowledge, and vision; the meal of the Tathāgata can never be exhausted.

Thereupon, they were all fully satiated by the rice in the bowl, yet the meal remained undiminished. After the bodhisattvas, great disciples, devas, and humans had eaten this food, their vital energy coursed through them and their bodies were at peace, just like those bodhisattvas in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Pervaded by that fragrance, all their pores were at peace, just as it is in the Land of Universal Fragrance, where the scent permeates even the eight difficult states of existence.
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti addressed the bodhisattvas from the Land of Universal Fragrance, saying:
"O sons of noble family!
"How does the Tathāgata Gandhottamakūṭa teach the Dharma?
That bodhisattva replied:

"In my land, the Tathāgata has no teaching through words or letters; rather, it is by means of fragrance that the bodhisattvas spontaneously enter into the practice of discipline. Each bodhisattva sits beneath a fragrant tree, and as they are all equally perfumed by its scent, they all attain the samādhi of all fragrant virtues. Being capable of attaining this concentration, the bodhisattvas remain entirely unattached in all their practices."
Those bodhisattvas asked Vimalakīrti,
"In what manner does the World-Honored One Śākyamuni manifest the Dharma?
Vimalakīrti replied:
"The people of this land are stubborn and difficult to transform; therefore, the Buddha speaks these words of severity for them:
'This leads to hell; this leads to the paths of animals, ghosts, and spirits; this is the retribution for evil conduct of body, speech, and mind.'"
As unwholesome and evil conduct increases, I therefore preach various essential teachings to transform their coarse and unruly minds.
It is like an elephant or horse that is stubborn and untamable; one must apply the bit and bridle and inflict the pain of the whip before it becomes well-trained and docile.
"Such a person who is difficult to transform and full of boastful pretension can only be brought into the discipline by means of words of admonition concerning all forms of suffering.
That Bodhisattva said:
"This is unprecedented!"

Just as the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, through his noble and great resolve, has endured to liberate those who are poor and greedy, and how even the bodhisattvas are able to labor with humility and remain in this buddha-field—it is truly marvelous!
Vimalakīrti said, "As you say,

the bodhisattvas in this land, by benefiting the people through great compassion during an age of the five corruptions, have practiced for more than hundreds of thousands of kalpas than those in that land."
Why is this so? Sons of good family!
This Sahā world possesses ten qualities of purity that do not exist in that land.
What are the ten?
One gathers in the poor through generosity;
one gathers in those who lack propriety through respect for the precepts.
By means of patience, one gathers in the violent;
by means of diligence, one gathers in the indolent;
by means of single-mindedness, one gathers in the distracted.
Using wisdom, one restrains erroneous knowledge;
through repentance, one transcends the eight difficulties;
by means of the Mahāyāna, one delights in universal practice.
To plant the roots of virtue in order to rescue those who lack virtue;
and to gather people together in order to deliver them.
These constitute the ten virtues.
"And yet, you resolve your mind to take them up.
That bodhisattva asked:
"By means of how many dharmas does one travel without injury from this Sahā world-system to other Buddha-fields?"
Vimalakīrti said:
"There are eight practices by which a bodhisattva remains free from injury as they depart from this Sahā world-system and travel to other Buddha-fields.
What are these eight?
To establish a sense of shame for the sake of the multitude, avoiding disorder and shunning vain expectations;
to take upon oneself suffering and endure strife for the sake of all people;
and to serve as the root of all virtues in order to rescue sentient beings.
He does not reject the assembly, and thus people love and respect him;
regarding sutras that the Bodhisattva has not yet heard, he consults and listens without confusion;
he does not envy the offerings given to others, nor does he plot for his own self-interest.
Constantly examining one's own faults and not disputing the shortcomings of others;
being foremost in self-restraint while studying the various sutras—

Why is this so? Because the Dharma gives birth to the Buddha-way, and from the Dharma all Buddhas emerge. One who is able to make offerings to this True Dharma is not one who merely intends to give; this should be understood in this way.
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas:

"In the distant past, incalculable and immeasurable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha in that world named Bhaiṣajyarāja (in the language of Han, 'Medicine King'), a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, a Buddha, a World-Honored One. His world was named Mahāviśuddha, and the kalpa was called Viśodhana."
At that time, O Śakra, Lord of Devas!
the lifespan of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja was thirty kalpas; his assembly of disciples numbered three hundred and sixty billion koṭis, and his bodhisattvas numbered one billion two hundred million.

At that time, there was a Wheel-Turning Sage King named Ratnacchattra, who possessed the seven treasures and ruled over the four continents; for five kalpas he served the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja, leading his officials and retinue to bestow all manner of comforts upon them.
In the fifth kalpa, the Holy King Ratnacchattra summoned his thousand sons and addressed them, saying:
"You have all seen the Tathāgata; you should together serve him and provide him with whatever brings him peace."

Thereupon, having heard their father the King’s command, the thousand sons all with peaceful harmony returned for another five kalpas to provide offerings to the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja, along with his retinue, bestowing all things to bring them peace and security.
The eldest prince, named Sunakṣatra, sat alone and reflected:
"Is there perhaps an offering that surpasses this?
A deva in the sky, receiving the Buddha’s holy intent, replied:
“O Noble One!
The offering of the Dharma surpasses all other offerings.
He then asked:
"What is meant by 'Dharma-offering'?
The deva replied,
"Why do you not go and ask the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja?"
"The Buddha shall explain to you the offering of the Dharma.
Thereupon, Prince Sunakṣatra rose immediately and went to the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja. Prostrating at the Buddha's feet, he asked:
"Regarding the 'offering of the Dharma' for those who perceive the Dharma, what does this mean?"
Buddha Bhaiṣajyarāja said:

"As for the Dharma-offering, it consists of the profound treasuries of the various sūtras and their deep words as taught by the Buddha—the refuge of all worlds. It is not something easily received or easily seen by those who are arrogant; yet, being subtle and formless, its meaning is simple and easy to understand."

The Bodhisattva’s treasury is cultivated until it reaches the various dhāraṇīs, sealed by the seal of the sūtras; this is not without principle. Its wheel is pure, entering the six perfections (pāramitās); one may properly take up and study the categories of the path, which are the matters of entering the purity of the Dharma and the correct state.

For the sake of others, he gives rise to great compassion and establishes great kindness; free from all extreme views, he perceives the Great Dependent Origination. He is neither person nor life-force, neither female nor male; like space, he is signless, wishless, and unconditioned. This is the practice of the stages of the Way and the juncture of the Wheel of Dharma, which is praised by hundreds of thousands of devas and humans; it is a vast treasury of Dharma that delivers many and embraces all beings.

It clearly elucidates the practices of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as the essential method for entering the Dharma that possesses meaning, leading one downward toward impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.

To have no transgressions in the precepts; for all such [transgressions] to be viewed with dread; to revere and look up to the Buddhas; to behold the cycle of birth and death yet not participate in it; to manifest parinirvāṇa together [with them]; to dwell in peace by practicing the subtle words of such scriptures as these; and to receive the Dharma through discernment and contemplation—this is the offering of the Dharma.
Furthermore, son of good family!

As for the offering of Dharma, it is to give rise to the Dharma through hearing the Dharma; the Dharma transforms into dependent origination, conforming to and departing from all extreme views. It is the non-arising of suchness, the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas, which is neither body nor person.
For these supreme causes and conditions, there is neither conflict nor grasping, as if there were no contention at all.
One abandons self-construction to rely upon the meaning rather than outward adornment;
one follows the sacred scriptures to rely upon wisdom rather than literary embellishment.
Entering into the meaning in every instance, he relies upon the sūtras and does not practice what is contrary to the meaning;
with what he has internalized, he relies upon the Dharma and does not follow the views of others.

He attains the non-appropriation of all dharmas and enters into the state of no-location; he extinguishes ignorance, extinguishes volitional formations, and extinguishes consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and the suffering of old age and death—everything is thus extinguished.
Thus ceasing and thus contemplating the arising of the twelve links of dependent origination, one experiences the sublime through inexhaustibility; that which others behold, one beholds not.
"Yes, son of good family!
This is called the unsurpassed offering of the Dharma.
"Thus it is, Lord of Devas!"

The Crown Prince Sunakṣatra, having heard the teaching on the offering of Dharma from the Buddha Bhaiṣajyarāja, immediately attained the stage of *ānulomikī-kṣānti*. He then took off his precious robe and covered the Buddha with it, saying:
"I am capable, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, of receiving and upholding the True Dharma, performing offerings of Dharma, and protecting this Path."
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will show compassion and establish me, so that I may subdue the enemies who are Māras and grasp the True Dharma of the Buddha.
That Buddha, knowing his inner disposition, spoke thus:
"In the final age, you shall guard the city of the Dharma."
At that time, Sunakṣatra, having seen the World-Honored One, out of faith in the household life, left home to receive the Way and diligently cultivated the roots of virtue.

Before long, through his diligent effort, he established himself in wholesome dharmas, gave rise to the five supernormal powers, attained mastery over all paths, and possessed uninterrupted eloquence.
Thereupon, after the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One, by the power of his wisdom, for a full ten kalpas he followed and distributed the Dharma-gifts turned by the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja.

At that time, the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra transformed one billion people, causing them to establish themselves in the Great Way; fourteen *koṭis* of people understood the vehicle of the disciples (*śrāvakayāna*), and immeasurable others attained rebirth in the heavens.
Thus it is, Śakra!
In times past, the king named Ratnacchattra is now the Buddha named Ratnasaṃbhava Tathāgata; and his crown prince, Sunakṣatra, was none other than myself.
The remaining sons shall all, within this Bhadrakalpa, attain the state of Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; these are the thousand Buddhas who will appear during this Bhadrakalpa.
From the time Krikin first became a Buddha until the final attainment by Ruci Tathāgata—O Śakra, Lord of Devas!
you should know this essential point:

in the past, my own person performed the offering of Dharma to all those Tathāgatas, thereby attaining the supreme transformation, the enduring transformation, the transformative power of aspiration, and the unsurpassed, incomparable transformation.
"Therefore, Śakra, Lord of Devas!
You should know that by means of this offering of the Dharma, one makes an offering to the Buddha.
Chapter 14: Entrustment to Maitreya At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying:

“Maitreya! This is called the ‘Chapter on Practicing the Buddha-way for Immeasurable Billions of Kalpas. You should distribute it accordingly and receive this kind of sutra established by the Buddha; after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, you shall propagate this path extensively.”

Why is this? Those who shall obtain it in future generations—sons and daughters of noble family, devas, nāgas, and gandharvas—who have planted roots of virtue and who, having previously excelled in practicing the path toward unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, have not yet heard or received this Dharma—upon hearing such sutras as these, will surely feel profound love and joy, and they shall receive this essential path of the Buddha upon the crown of their heads.
Furthermore, Maitreya!
You should benefit these sons of noble family by manifesting this sutra text for them.
There are two seals of a bodhisattva; what are the two?
There is the seal of those who delight in miscellaneous phrases and ornate embellishments, and there is the seal of those who enter the profound Dharma and wondrous transformations.
If one takes pleasure in miscellaneous phrases and ornaments, you should know that such a person belongs to the class of the Āyītián Bodhisattvas.

If one obtains this profound sutra and receives it widely, practicing it without repeated fear and being able to transmit it upon hearing it, you should know that this bodhisattva has long cultivated the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
Furthermore, there are four matters by which Ājīvika ascetics squander their efforts in vain.
What are these four?
To be startled and suspicious upon hearing a sutra they have never heard before; to fail to offer encouragement or assistance; and to exclusively increase disorder.
"I have never heard of this; from where does it come?
O son of good family!

One who understands the profound Dharma well and delights in eloquently expounding the subtle, yet does not learn from others, and though dwelling near [the teacher], is disrespectful and lacks single-minded devotion, and engages in destructive conduct therein—these are the four reasons why Ājñātakauṇḍinya was empty and wasted, failing to attain the patience of the profound Dharma (gambhīra-dharma-kṣānti).
Furthermore, Maitreya!
There are two practices by which a bodhisattva, despite understanding profound dharmas, remains empty and exhausted.
What are these two?
To dwell in remote regions and fail to maintain constant conduct; to treat people with contempt through stinginess and ignorance, refusing to accept or recite [the teachings], nor seeking them out;

and when there are those who possess profound understanding and study the deep Dharma, to respond with arrogance, greed, and jealousy, being unable to welcome others nor practice the gift of Dharma—these constitute the second [set of faults].

"Although they understand the profound Dharma, they still waste their efforts in vain; they cannot quickly draw near, nor can they give rise to the patience regarding dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is unprecedented! Indeed it is so!"
World-Honored One!

Regarding the virtuous words of the Tathāgata, I shall distance myself from such evils in order to protect the practice of the Tathāgata’s factors of enlightenment throughout countless billions of kalpas.

If a son of noble family enters into such sūtras as these, he shall be enabled to take from them with his own hands whatever he desires to contemplate; and if he contemplates and upholds such sūtras as these, he shall transmit and show them to his fellow students, explaining them clearly and extensively.
At that time, World-Honored One!
those who obtain such a sutra as this and joyfully transmit it to others should be known as bodhisattvas established by Maitreya.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, Maitreya!”
"The Tathāgata rejoices on our behalf; well said are these words.
Thereupon, all the bodhisattvas together raised their voices and said:

"After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, wherever we may be in various buddha-fields, we shall come here to disseminate the Buddha-way and instruct our fellow students according to what they delight in."
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings addressed the Buddha,
saying: "Wherever there may be, World-Honored One,
villages, towns, cities, or states where those who practice such profound sutras and dharmas reside."
I shall lead my various officials and attendants to the place where the Dharma is being preached to protect the teaching of the Dharma.
Within a range of one hundred yojanas, I shall cause all beings to hear and see the preaching of the Dharma, ensuring that no one who seeks an opportunity to find fault can gain the advantage.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"Receive this Dharma of the sutra, uphold it, recite it, and proclaim it to others.
Ānanda said:
"Yes, we shall receive this sutra and disseminate it among the masses.
Furthermore, World-Honored One,
what should this sutra be named?"
Furthermore, by what title should it be upheld?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“It is called ‘The Teaching of Vimalakīrti,’ and it is also called ‘The Designation of the Inconceivable Dharma-Gate. You should uphold it as such.”
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, there was no one who did not joyfully accept them.

With the Venerable Vimalakīrti and Mañjuśrī as their leaders, the assembly of bodhisattvas, great disciples, and all the hosts of Māras heard what the Buddha had taught and were all filled with great joy.
